faq: Do I need a developer account first?

You need a Chrome Web Store developer account to publish, which carries a small one-time fee paid to Google. We can guide you through setup, and we submit from your account if you add us as a collaborator.
Will it work in browsers other than Chrome?
Manifest V3 extensions run in Chrome and Edge with little change. Firefox and Safari need extra packaging, so ask us and we quote that part separately in writing before we start.
Yes. You receive the complete source code and a build guide, and the extension lives in your own account. We keep no hidden access once the order is closed.
Do you promise the store will approve it?

No one can promise that. We build to the Chrome Web Store rules, keep permissions minimal and explain them plainly, which gives the review the best chance. If a reviewer asks for changes, we help fix them.

desc:
Chrome and Edge extension development from Ecom Swift LLC takes your idea from a short written feature list to a tested Manifest V3 extension, with the store package, privacy wording and full source code handed over.

## How does Chrome and Edge extension development work?

Chrome and Edge extension development means writing a small web-technology program that runs inside the browser and adds a tool the user chose to install. Both browsers read the same Manifest V3 format, so one well-built codebase can serve both stores. The code is mostly HTML, CSS and JavaScript, plus a manifest file that tells the browser what the extension may do.

Most failed extension projects do not fail on code. They fail because the idea was vague, the permissions were too broad or the store package was rushed. Building in a clear order avoids all three.

## Why a planned build gives a better product

An extension lives in a crowded toolbar and is judged in seconds. If the popup is confusing, the permissions look excessive or the first click does nothing, the user removes it. A planned build starts with one job that the extension does clearly, then adds features only when they support that job.

Planning also protects your budget. When the feature list is agreed in writing before the first line of code, changes are visible and priced fairly, and you are not surprised by a missing screen at the end.

## What a finished extension should include

- A manifest that asks only for the permissions the features really use.
- A background service worker that wakes when needed and sleeps otherwise.
- A popup that explains itself on the first open.
- An options page where users change settings and see them saved.
- Clean icons in the sizes the browsers require.
- Content scripts only where the feature must touch a web page.
- Safe storage for settings, with clear defaults.
- A privacy policy that matches what the code actually does.
- Store screenshots, a title and a description written for the people who search.

## How we build it

First, you describe the problem in plain words and we turn it into a short feature list that you approve in writing. Then we write the code, design the popup and settings, and test on real pages in Chrome and Edge, including a clean browser profile so we see what a new user sees.

The three packages grow in scope. Basic delivers one core feature and one popup, packaged for the store. Standard adds more features, an options page, saved settings, icons, store images and drafted privacy text. Premium adds a side panel, a connection to one API or backend, store listing text and submission from your own developer account, plus a period of bug fixes after release.

You receive the source code, a store-ready package and a short handover note explaining how the project is organized.

## Do and avoid when planning an extension

**Do:**
- Describe one clear job for the extension in a single sentence.
- Collect examples of the sites or pages where it should work.
- Decide early whether users need an account.
- Test on a second computer before you submit.
- Write the privacy answers from the real behavior of the code.

**Avoid:**
- Asking for access to every site when two would do.
- Adding features just because a competitor has them.
- Loading code from a remote server, which stores restrict.
- Collecting data you have no plan to use.
- Submitting the first build without a review of the listing text.

## Who this is for

It suits a founder with an idea for a browser tool who has no developer. It suits an agency that wants to add a branded extension to a client's service. And it suits a website owner who wants a helper tool, such as a page saver or price checker, for their own customers.

## What we need from you

Send a short brief: what the extension does, who uses it and which sites or pages matter. Share any sketches, brand colors and a logo if you have them. If you plan to publish, create a developer account with the store you choose, because the listing must belong to you.

We never ask for passwords. For the final upload, you can add us with the access level the store dashboard allows, or upload the package yourself with our written steps. After you order, we reply with a checklist and a draft feature list for your approval.
